idiom_name: MonoBehaviour.Update() driven by Unity's player loop
implementation_notes: Unity's player loop owns the collection and the walk: 'Update is called every frame, if the MonoBehaviour is enabled', and Time.deltaTime is the elapsed time since the previous call; a component therefore implements only its step, and enabling or disabling the component enables or disables that step. What replaces the classic structure: the scene's component registry replaces the entity list and the engine's player loop replaces the driver - writing your own manager beside it is a second dispatch layer over the same objects. MonoGame/XNA offers the same shape with an explicit collection (Game.Components, GameComponent.Update); a plain .NET simulation without an engine has no dispatch at all and hand-writes the list walk, passing dt explicitly.
pitfalls: Order among Update methods follows Unity's execution order, not creation order; per-frame dependencies between components must be made explicit (script execution order) instead of assumed.
Time.deltaTime is the rendered frame step: physics and accumulators belong in FixedUpdate, and using deltaTime there double-applies time when FixedUpdate runs several times per frame.
Update runs on the main thread, so one blocking call or long loop stalls every other component for that frame.

Destroying an object inside Update is deferred to the end of the frame while disabling a component is immediate, and thousands of small Update methods cost managed call overhead at scale - batch or use jobs when counts grow.

variants.name: MonoGame Game.Components (XNA lineage)
variants.implementation_notes: MonoGame's Game 'runs a game loop that calls Update(GameTime) and Draw(GameTime)' and exposes 'a collection of game components attached to this Game' (Components); each GameComponent implements Update(GameTime) and the framework walks the collection every frame - the XNA lineage Nystrom names in the pattern's See Also section. What replaces the classic structure: Game is the driver and Components the ordered collection, so the pattern reduces to implementing the step and registering the component; use it for non-Unity .NET games and tools where the framework should own the walk without adopting a scene-component model. Ordering is the collection's order, and components may be added or removed at runtime under the framework's rules.
pitfalls: Components are only updated while registered: removing one stops its step silently, and re-adding restores it.
ElapsedGameTime equals TargetElapsedTime under a fixed time step and varies otherwise; use the value you are handed and never assume a constant dt.
Component order is registration order, so dependencies between components need explicit ordering or a two-phase update.
